solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Stiff run part way through dense thicket

indicators.note: a thing part way through something sits inside it, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: a copse is a small thick wood
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone stiff from exertion runs partway into a dense thicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like an adjective about aching legs, but it is the slang noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff is slang for a dead body, especially in crime fiction.

clue.text: On the other hand, setter goes in fencing English sportsman

indicators.note: to fence something is to enclose it, so one word wraps round the letter for English

blocks.note: or introduces an alternative, as 'on the other hand' does
the setter refers to themselves as I
to enter is to go in
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English fencer takes to the piste, with the setter joining in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' suggests the sword sport, but it is the containment signal: ENTER goes round E.
explanation.definitionFit: An orienteer is a competitor who races across country with map and compass, so one kind of sportsman.

clue.text: Craft in the style of Harry?

blocks.note: Harry Potter, the boy wizard of the novels
the suffix -y forms adjectives meaning like or in the manner of

explanation.surface: A question about some craft or wizardry done the way Harry would do it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'Potter-y', something in Harry Potter's manner; 'Craft' doubles as the wizard's craft in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Making ceramic pots and vessels from fired clay is a traditional handicraft.

clue.text: Attention — see ya later, at the end

indicators.note: points to the final letter of each of the preceding words in turn

blocks.note: the closing letters of the three casual farewell words

explanation.surface: A casual 'see ya later' tossed off at the end of a conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: To lend an ear or have someone's ear is to give them notice and listening.

clue.text: Tell tales about husband — note claptrap

indicators.note: about means round, so the word for telling tales goes around the letter

blocks.note: to blab is to reveal secrets
H is the abbreviation for husband
lah is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone gossips about a husband, but you should note it's all nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive words for empty, pretentious or meaningless talk.

clue.text: Resisting poor performers, take on county

blocks.note: bucking a trend is resisting it
hams are bad, overacting actors
to take on staff is to hire them

explanation.surface: A manager refuses to drop weak performers and instead takes on a whole county.
explanation.walkthrough: BUCKINGHAMSHIRE is an English county north-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is one of the home counties, an administrative region of southern England.

clue.text: Quick movements exhausted abnormal limb on climbing small mammal

indicators.note: an exhausted thing has been emptied, so only the outside letters of the next word survive
in a down entry climbing means reading upward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
a leg is a limb
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
the otter is a river-dwelling mammal

explanation.surface: A worn-out creature with a deformed leg scrambles up past a small animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick movements' looks like the scramble in the surface, but it is musical: the parts of a symphony.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegretto is a fairly brisk musical passage, so pieces in that tempo are lively movements.

clue.text: Eg Munro with top bagged from moorland below

indicators.note: the top letter is taken away, bagged like a trophy, from the following word

blocks.note: a Munro is a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet, and ben is the Scots word for a mountain
a heath is open moorland

explanation.surface: A hillwalker bags a Munro summit with the moorland stretched out below.
explanation.walkthrough: Hillwalkers speak of 'bagging' Munros when they reach the summit, so 'top bagged' fits the surface perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are prepositions meaning lower down than or underneath something.

clue.text: Sadly incomplete doctor's mission

indicators.note: something incomplete is missing its last part, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: alas is an expression of sorrow
MO is a medical officer

explanation.surface: A doctor's overseas mission sadly left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alamo in Texas was a Spanish mission before its famous siege in 1836.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo was founded as a Spanish Catholic mission church in San Antonio.

clue.text: This quirky Shakespearean jester barely famous in the past

indicators.note: quirky means odd or unconventional, so the preceding word's letters are rearranged
barely means stripped bare, so the jester's name loses its outer letters

blocks.note: taken as written
Yorick is the dead jester whose skull Hamlet holds

explanation.surface: An odd Shakespearean clown was barely known in his day.
explanation.definitionFit: Something historic is notable in history, important enough to be remembered from earlier times.

clue.text: Secure gold carriage

blocks.note: to land a deal or catch is to secure it
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Lock away the gold in a carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle with a folding hood.

clue.text: Railing in abandoned house giving out

indicators.note: an abandoned building is left empty, so only the outside letters of the next word remain
out here means out of order or awry, so all the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Railings in a derelict house are giving way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Railing' looks like a fence but is the verb for ranting against something.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail against something and to inveigh against it both mean to protest bitterly and at length.

clue.text: Good former French footballer, almost dying, finally adding expensive cover

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the surname's last letter is dropped
finally picks out only the closing letter of the word before it

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
old means former, as in old boss
Michel Platini, France's star midfielder of the 1980s
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A once-great French footballer, nearly dead, adds a costly covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin layer of gold over a cheaper metal is a costly finish, and the phrase also means unnecessary embellishment.

clue.text: Neural extension centres in ataxic sartorius and supinator

indicators.note: the centres of words are their middle letters, taken from each in turn

blocks.note: the middle two letters of a six-letter word
middle letter
middle letter

explanation.surface: Medical jargon about a nerve fibre running through an uncoordinated thigh muscle and a forearm muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: Ataxic means lacking coordination; the sartorius is a thigh muscle and the supinator a forearm muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: An axon is the long thread-like projection of a nerve cell that carries impulses away from it.

clue.text: Bulgarian money linked to variable tax

blocks.note: the lev is Bulgaria's currency
y is a standard algebraic variable

explanation.surface: Bulgarian currency tied to a variable rate of tax.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy is a charge or duty imposed by authority, a form of taxation.

clue.text: Stupid person, selfish type cycling in first place

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round in a loop, so the front letter goes to the back
in places the cycled word inside the word for first place

blocks.note: a hogger is one who hogs things
being in the lead is first place

explanation.surface: A selfish cyclist hogging first place in a race is an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' fits a bike race in the surface, but it moves the first letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Loggerhead is an archaic word for a blockhead or dolt, surviving in the idiom 'at loggerheads'.

clue.text: Terrible stain surrounding principal Bolshevik?

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so the next word's letters are messed up
surrounding means going round, so the rearranged letters wrap round the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
arch- as a prefix means chief, as in archenemy

explanation.surface: A dreadful mark on the record of a leading revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a Bolshevik is only loosely an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolsheviks were revolutionaries seeking to overthrow the state, so loosely rebels against authority and order.

clue.text: Victorious motorbike company magnate making regular appearances

indicators.note: regular appearances means showing up at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: Triumph is a British motorcycle maker
second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: The successful tycoon behind a motorcycle firm keeps popping up in public.
explanation.definitionFit: Triumphant describes someone who has won or is rejoicing at success.

clue.text: Annul vacuous rules, breaking free

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so only the outer letters of the following word are kept
breaking smashes the order of the letters so they can be put back differently

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Scrapping empty regulations means breaking free.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsnarl a tangle is to free it from knots and disentangle it.

clue.text: Seat, maybe for carrying unknown ruler

indicators.note: a vehicle carrying something has it inside, so the unknown goes into it

blocks.note: SEAT is a Spanish car manufacturer, so a Seat is an example of a car
z is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A chair might be meant for a monarch nobody has heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' looks like a chair or throne, but it is the Spanish car brand.
explanation.definitionFit: A czar or tsar was the emperor of Russia, an absolute monarch.

clue.text: Facetiously, girl from El Salvador wearing leather riding gear

indicators.note: whoever wears clothing is inside it, so the country code goes within the gear

blocks.note: chaps are leather leggings worn by riders and cowboys
ES is El Salvador's international vehicle code

explanation.surface: A Salvadoran cowgirl rides out in leather chaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapess is a jokey feminine of chap, used humorously for a woman or girl.

clue.text: Circus attraction in London aching to go west

indicators.note: in an across entry going west means travelling right to left, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: sore means aching

explanation.surface: A circus act in London whose performers are aching to head west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circus' suggests a big top, but it is Piccadilly Circus, the London junction whose famous winged statue is known as EROS.
explanation.definitionFit: The statue atop the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain in Piccadilly Circus is popularly called by the Greek love god's name.

clue.text: River horse caught

indicators.note: caught means picked up by the ear, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a roan is a horse with a coat flecked with white

explanation.surface: A river horse, perhaps a hippo, gets caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River horse' wants to be a hippopotamus; 'River' is the definition and 'horse' the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône flows from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean, one of Europe's major waterways.

clue.text: Support fool with primarily ignorant attitude

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter only of the word that follows

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
first letter of the word
a stance is an attitude or position

explanation.surface: Backing a fool whose outlook is basically ignorant.
explanation.definitionFit: Assistance is help or aid given to someone, which is backing them up.

clue.text: Holding stuff back, king of France discloses Japanese letters

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the word for stuff reads in the other direction
holding means having inside, so the French word wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: roi is French for king
to jam is to stuff or cram

explanation.surface: A secretive French king finally reveals something written in Japanese.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaji is the system of writing Japanese in the Roman alphabet.

clue.text: Undaunted, Independent printed rubbish

indicators.note: rubbish here means badly done, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for Independent
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Independent newspaper bravely printed rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The Independent is a British newspaper, which makes 'printed rubbish' a plausible jibe.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrepid means fearless and bold, unshaken by danger.

clue.text: Dump hint

blocks.note: first meaning: a rubbish site, or to unload
second meaning: a useful pointer or suggestion

explanation.walkthrough: A tip is British for a rubbish dump; the other sense is advice.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a rubbish heap and also a small piece of useful advice.

clue.text: Item that reveals National Curriculum avoids carelessness

indicators.note: to avoid something is to steer clear of it, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: NC is the abbreviation for the National Curriculum taught in English schools
negligence is lack of proper care

explanation.surface: An exposé of how the school curriculum dodges responsibility for carelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: N and C are removed separately, not as a pair, from the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A negligee is a flimsy, often sheer nightgown, so a garment that shows off more than it hides.

clue.text: Assumes props will welcome international

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: posts are supports or props
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A rugby side assumes its props will welcome an international player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Props' suggests rugby forwards, but here it means supports.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit something is to put it forward as a premise, taking it as given.
